Suicide Risk Assessment

screening by age · ideation, plan and intent · risk and protective factors · level of care · antidepressant warningIs the risk imminent, and what does that decide about the level of care?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Ask directly asking does not cause or worsen suicidal thinking
  • Plan with intent to act, or uncertain whether he will act hospitalize, involuntarily if he refuses
  • Thoughts without plan or intent safety plan, intensive outpatient treatment, follow-up
What it is

A bedside assessment of ideation, plan and intent that sets the level of care

Driver

Ideation with a plan and intent to act risk factors outweighing protective ones

Low cerebrospinal fluid 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), the main serotonin metabolite, is associated with suicidal behavior

Triggers

Prior attempt (non-modifiable; the strongest predictor)

Firearm at home, alcohol or drugs, hopelessness, a recent loss, living alone

Chain

Passive thoughts active thoughts plan rehearsal or preparatory acts

Each step raises the risk

Insights

A prior attempt outranks a firearm or alcohol: both are real but lesser, and modifiable; in the acute setting, active alcohol or drug use (disinhibition) weighs more than the other static factors: age, sex and family history

Intoxicated or delirious no valid assessment until cognition is intact

Risk and protective factorsdetail behind the triggers
StaticPrior attempt, age (adolescents and young adults; over 70 has the highest rates), male sex for death (females attempt more), family history of suicide or psychiatric illness
ModifiablePlan or intent, access to weapons or medications, intoxication or substance use (disinhibition), impulsivity, psychosis or agitation, psychiatric or medical illness, stopping treatment, hopelessness, a recent stressor, living alone
FirearmsA firearm at home is an independent risk factor, about 3 times the risk of death by suicide; the most common method in the US
ProtectiveEffective mental health care, connectedness, beliefs that discourage suicide

Risk factors in one mnemonic: Risk factor mnemonicSex (male), Age (teenage or elderly), Depression, Previous attempt (the highest risk), Ethanol or drug use, Rational thinking impaired (psychosis), Sickness (medical illness), Organized plan, No spouse or other support, Stated future intent.

2Urgent risks
ImminentA specific plan with intent to act now, rehearsal or preparatory acts, few or no protective factors

If he refuses admission, choose involuntary hospitalization under local law.

ImpairedIntoxicated or delirious, cannot answer questions about a plan

If cognition is impaired, choose one-to-one observation with suicide precautions until he is sober, then the full assessment.

3Differential
Which level of risk, most tempting first
PictureFingerprintDecides it
High (imminent) riskFrequent thoughts, a specific plan, intent to act now, rehearsal or preparationIntent to act now; hospitalize even if he looks calm
Uncertain intentSuicidal thoughts, and no one can say whether he will actUncertainty is not low risk; emergency hospitalization
Low (nonimminent) riskPassive or infrequent thoughts, no plan or intent, protective factorsNo plan and no intent; outpatient care, not admission
Assessment not yet validIntoxication or deliriumCognition impaired; a steady gait does not replace the assessment
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Age 12 or older, routine visitUniversal screeningValidated screen (eg, Ask Suicide-Screening Questions); a positive screen gets a brief safety assessment
Age 8 to 11Screen when clinically indicatedUnder 8: not indicated, but assess if warning signs
Adult with current depression or a prior attemptTargeted screeningAsk directly
Minor with active concerns for suicideSafety outranks privacyTelling a parent or guardian is permissible; hospitalize for safety
Paranoid and impulsive, with a gun at home; no threats, no suicidal or homicidal ideationAcute risk to others and to himselfRestrict access to the firearm first, within an outpatient safety plan WhyAccess to the firearm poses the most immediate risk. Notifying others is not needed without homicidal ideation or specific threats. Safety contracts have not proven efficacious in preventing violence. With multiple acute risk factors, hospitalization should be considered.
Pause point
Calm, sober patient with a rehearsed plan Read as safe because he promises to stay safe Intent and preparation set the risk; a no-suicide contract does not prevent suicide → Admit, involuntarily if he refuses
6Severity
Risk tier and level of care
TierFeaturesLevel of care
LowNo or infrequent thoughts; no apparent plan or intent; few risk factors, many protective onesOutpatient: safety plan, means removal, treatment, follow-up
UncertainThoughts present; whether he will act is unclearEmergency hospitalization
High (imminent)Frequent thoughts, specific plan, intent to act now, rehearsal, few protective factorsInpatient hospitalization; involuntary if he refuses
7Treatment
1

Lowthoughts without plan or intent

Collaborative safety plan: coping, supports, emergency and crisis contacts; discuss removing means, with family help if he agrees

Treat the condition and arrange follow-up; intensive outpatient treatment, not admission. Not a Why notA promise not to harm himself. It does not prevent suicide; a safety plan replaces it..

2

Highspecific plan with imminent intent, rehearsal or preparation, or uncertain whether he will act

Inpatient hospitalization with precautions: remove hazards, one-to-one sitter
3

Refuseshe refuses admission

Involuntary hospitalization under local law
By situation
SituationDo
Minor with active suicidal ideationHospitalize for safety; telling a parent or guardian is permissible
Firearm or stockpiled medication at homeDiscuss removing access, with family help if he agrees
Depression driving the riskTreat the condition driving the risk
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
Starting an antidepressant such as a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), especially in a child, adolescent or young adultMonitor closely for worsening and new suicidal thoughts; Was it the drug or a new stressor?Improvement on the drug before a new stressor makes the drug a less likely cause of the suicidal thoughts; look for the stressor and for substance use. The evidence that the drug causes suicidal thoughts is inconclusive, and expert consensus favors treating.
Low risk, managed as an outpatientFollow-up visits; reassess if high-risk features appear
Practice
  1. 52-year-old man, depressed since his divorce 6 months ago lives alone; drinks most nights; keeps a handgun at home overdosed on purpose 2 years ago wishes he would not wake up; no plan · BP 138/86 mm Hg → His previous attempt → a prior attempt is the most predictive risk factor for another attempt; access to a firearm and alcohol use are real but lesser risk factors, and both are modifiable through means removal and treatment
  2. 34-year-old woman says she will swallow her saved pills tonight gave her cat to a friend and wrote letters to her children says nothing will change her mind; no reasons for living sober · alert, oriented · HR 92/min → Inpatient hospitalization → a specific plan with intent to act now, preparatory acts and few or no protective factors is high, imminent risk: recommend inpatient care with precautions; outpatient safety planning is for low risk, and no-suicide contracts do not prevent suicide
  3. 29-year-old man found on a bridge railing, now in the emergency department still plans to jump when released; refuses admission no alcohol or drugs today; urine toxicology negative alert and oriented · BP 132/84 mm Hg → Involuntary hospitalization → high, imminent risk with a rehearsed method and ongoing intent: if he refuses hospitalization, pursue involuntary admission under local law; any discharge leaves an imminent plan untreated
  4. 45-year-old woman with depression sometimes wishes she could sleep and not wake no plan, no intent, never harmed herself close to her sister; active in her church; no firearms at home alert, oriented · BP 118/74 mm Hg → Safety plan and follow-up → passive thoughts without plan or intent, few risk factors and strong protective factors are low risk: build a safety plan with supports and crisis contacts, treat the depression and arrange follow-up; no-suicide contracts are not effective
  5. 14-year-old girl at a sports physical no complaints; grades good; plays soccer seen alone for part of the visit; parents in the waiting room T 36.8 °C · BP 108/66 mm Hg · examination normal → Validated suicide risk screen → universal suicide risk screening is recommended from age 12, with tools such as the Ask Suicide-Screening Questions; screening only when indicated applies to ages 8 to 11
  6. 38-year-old man brought in after saying he wants to die slurred speech, unsteady; blood alcohol 280 mg/dL cannot follow questions about a plan HR 104/min · BP 142/90 mm Hg · oxygen saturation 96% → Observe one-to-one until sober → a risk assessment needs intact cognition: while intoxicated, manage him under close one-to-one observation with suicide precautions until the assessment can be done, then complete it; a steady gait does not replace it
Pairs with Major Depressive Disorder: treat the condition driving the risk. Adolescent Confidentiality: when safety outranks privacy.
Transferable rule

Plan, intent, preparation, and risk and protective factors set the level of care; a prior attempt is the most predictive risk factor.
